title: Galaxies and the Big Bang: the universe is growing, and it had a beginning

summary.text: Almost every galaxy is moving away from us, and the further away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away. This happens because the space between the galaxies is stretching. Run the stretching backwards, and everything was once packed close together and very hot, about 13.8 billion years ago. Scientists call that beginning the Big Bang. Galaxies come in different shapes, from flat spirals to smooth ovals, and their light takes so long to reach us that we see far galaxies as they were long ago.
summary.art: A night sky full of galaxies of different shapes, spirals, ovals and shapeless clouds of stars. In front, a child holds up a balloon with bindis stuck on it, and dotted arrows show the bindis moving apart.

intro.hook: Astronomers have found that almost every galaxy in the sky is moving away from us. Does that mean we are at the centre of the universe?
intro.text: In this unit you stick bindis on a balloon and blow it bigger, to see how things move when the space between them grows. You meet the shapes that galaxies come in, and test how one galaxy can look like different shapes. You find out how Henrietta Leavitt and Edwin Hubble showed that our Milky Way is one galaxy among very many. And you learn why looking far away means looking back in time.
intro.art: A half-blown balloon with six coloured bindis on it, next to a ruler and a piece of thread, on a kitchen table.

outcomes: I can say what a galaxy is, and name the main shapes: spiral, barred spiral, elliptical and irregular.
I can explain, using my balloon test, why far galaxies move away from us faster than near ones.
I can explain why galaxies moving away from us does not mean we are at the centre of the universe.
I can say what the Big Bang was, and give two clues that the universe had a hot beginning.
I can explain why we see a far galaxy as it was long ago, not as it is now.
I can tell how Henrietta Leavitt and Edwin Hubble found that the Milky Way is one galaxy among many.
I can say what scientists still do not know, such as what came before the Big Bang.

terms.meaning: A huge group of stars, gas and dust, held together by gravity. A galaxy can have billions of stars.
terms.example: Our Sun is one of the stars in a galaxy called the Milky Way.
terms.art: A spiral galaxy with a bright middle and curling arms, with a tiny arrow pointing to one dot labelled 'a star like our Sun'.

terms.meaning: The galaxy we live in. From a dark place, we see part of it as a faint glowing band across the night sky.
terms.example: The Milky Way has between 100 and 400 billion stars, and it is about 100,000 light-years across.
terms.art: A faint milky band of light across a dark sky above a hill village with a few dim lamps.

terms.meaning: A galaxy shaped like a flat disc, with arms that curl out from a bright middle. New stars are being made in the arms.
terms.example: The Andromeda galaxy and the Whirlpool galaxy are spiral galaxies.
terms.art: A face-on spiral galaxy with two curling arms dotted with blue stars.

terms.meaning: A spiral galaxy with a straight bar of stars across its middle. The arms start from the ends of the bar.
terms.example: Our Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy.
terms.art: A spiral galaxy with a bright straight bar across the centre and arms curling from each end.

terms.meaning: A galaxy shaped like a smooth oval or ball of stars, with no arms. Most of its stars are old, and few new ones are being made.
terms.example: M87 is a giant elliptical galaxy, about 55 million light-years away.
terms.art: A smooth, glowing, yellowish oval of stars, brightest in the middle and fading at the edges.

terms.meaning: A galaxy with no clear shape. Many irregular galaxies are small.
terms.example: The Large Magellanic Cloud is a small irregular galaxy close to the Milky Way.
terms.art: A patchy, shapeless cloud of stars with pink and blue glowing patches.

terms.meaning: How far light travels in one year, about 9.5 million million kilometres. It is a distance, not a length of time.
terms.example: The Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away, so its light takes about 2.5 million years to reach us.
terms.art: A beam of light leaving a star and travelling a very long line, with a calendar showing one year at the other end.

terms.meaning: The space between the galaxies is growing all the time, so galaxies far apart get further and further apart.
terms.example: A galaxy twice as far away from us is moving away about twice as fast.
terms.art: Galaxies drawn on a grid of lines, and the same galaxies on a bigger grid, with the gaps between them wider.

terms.meaning: The name for the start of the universe as we know it. About 13.8 billion years ago, everything was packed close together and very hot, and it has been stretching and cooling ever since.
terms.example: The hydrogen in the water you drink was made in the first few minutes after the Big Bang.
terms.art: A timeline from a bright white-hot glow on the left to galaxies spread out on the right.

terms.meaning: A very faint glow of microwaves that reaches us from every direction in the sky. It is light left over from when the whole universe was hot.
terms.example: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found it by accident in 1965 with a big radio antenna.
terms.art: A large horn-shaped antenna on a field, pointing at the sky, with faint wavy lines arriving from every direction.

terms.meaning: When light travels across stretching space, its waves are stretched too. This shifts the light towards red. Astronomers measure it to find how fast a galaxy is moving away.
terms.example: Light from very far galaxies is stretched so much that it arrives as infrared light, which our eyes cannot see.
terms.art: A wavy line of light leaving a galaxy with short blue waves, and arriving at Earth with long red waves.

terms.meaning: A kind of star that gets brighter and dimmer again and again, in a steady rhythm. The slower it blinks, the brighter it really is.
terms.example: Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in the Andromeda galaxy, and used it to show how far away Andromeda is.
terms.art: The same star drawn five times in a row, bright, dim, dim, bright, dim, like a slow blinking lamp.

terms.meaning: A cloud of gas and dust in space. Before 1923, astronomers also used this word for the faint spiral smudges that turned out to be other galaxies.
terms.example: The Orion Nebula is a real cloud of gas inside our galaxy, where new stars are being made.
terms.art: A glowing pink and blue cloud of gas with a few bright young stars inside it.

explanations.definition: A galaxy is a huge group of stars, gas and dust, held together by its own gravity.
explanations.description: Stars are not spread evenly through space. They gather in galaxies, with huge empty gaps between the galaxies. Our Sun is one star in the Milky Way. The Milky Way has between 100 and 400 billion stars. Light takes about 100,000 years to cross it. There are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the part of the universe we can see, and perhaps many more. In 2022, the Webb space telescope photographed a patch of sky as small as a grain of sand held at arm's length. It held thousands of galaxies.
examples: The Andromeda galaxy, our nearest big neighbour, has about a trillion stars.
The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies close to the Milky Way. They can be seen by eye from the far south of the Earth.
explanations.art: Our Milky Way drawn as a spiral, with a tiny dot labelled 'the Sun', and other galaxies far away around it.
explanations.context: This card explains what a galaxy is.

explanations.definition: Astronomers sort galaxies by shape: spiral, barred spiral, elliptical and irregular. Edwin Hubble made this sorting in 1926.
explanations.description: A spiral galaxy is a flat, spinning disc with a bright bulge in the middle and arms that curl out. A barred spiral has a straight bar of stars across its middle. An elliptical galaxy is a smooth oval or ball of stars with no arms. An irregular galaxy has no clear shape. Spirals still have lots of gas, so new stars keep being made in their arms. The youngest, hottest stars are blue, so spiral arms look blue. Elliptical galaxies have little gas left, so few new stars are made, and their older stars make them look yellow or red. A disc looks different from different sides. Seen from the top, it is round. Seen from the side, it is a thin line.
examples: The Pinwheel galaxy is a spiral we see from the top, so its arms show clearly.
The Sombrero galaxy is a spiral we see almost from the side. It looks like a hat with a dark band of dust across it.
M87 is a giant elliptical galaxy. The first photo of a black hole, in 2019, was of the black hole at its centre.
explanations.art: Four galaxy shapes side by side, labelled: spiral, barred spiral, elliptical and irregular.
explanations.context: This card explains the shapes of galaxies.

explanations.description: A spiral galaxy spins, but not like a wheel. Stars near the middle go round in less time than stars further out. So you might expect the arms to wind up tighter and tighter, and vanish. They don't. Astronomers have more than one explanation, and different galaxies may have different reasons.
examples: The Sun takes about 230 million years to go once round the Milky Way.
The Whirlpool galaxy has very clear arms, and a smaller galaxy is passing close to it.

perspectives.who: The traffic-jam idea (Chia-Chiao Lin and Frank Shu, 1964)
perspectives.explanation: The arms are like a slow traffic jam that goes round the galaxy. Stars and gas move into an arm, crowd together for a while, and move out again. The crowding squeezes gas clouds, so new stars are made there.
In many galaxies, arms form, stretch, fade and form again, as the galaxy spins. Computer models of spinning galaxies show arms like this.
A nearby galaxy can pull on a spiral as it passes, and stir up strong arms. The Whirlpool galaxy may have got its arms this way.

explanations.art: A spiral galaxy with cars drawn along one arm, bunched up like a traffic jam, and stars moving in and out of it.
explanations.context: This card is about a question astronomers still argue about.

explanations.definition: The space between galaxies is growing all the time. So distant galaxies are moving away from each other, and the further apart two galaxies are, the faster they move apart.
explanations.description: In 1929, Edwin Hubble showed that far galaxies are moving away from us, and the further away they are, the faster they go. Georges Lemaître had worked this out two years earlier. It does not mean we are at the centre. The galaxies are not flying through space away from one spot. The space between them is stretching, everywhere at once. So from any galaxy, all the others seem to move away. This happens only across the huge gaps between groups of galaxies. Galaxies themselves do not grow, because gravity holds their stars together. The Earth, your house and your body do not stretch either. Our nearest big neighbour, Andromeda, is even moving towards us, because gravity pulls the two galaxies together.
examples: On a balloon, every bindi moves away from every other bindi as the balloon grows, and the far ones move the most.
A galaxy twice as far away from us moves away about twice as fast.
Andromeda is coming towards us at about 110 kilometres every second.
explanations.art: The same group of galaxies drawn twice, the second time with every gap bigger, and arrows from one galaxy to all the others.
explanations.context: This card explains what the bindi balloon showed.

explanations.concept: The Big Bang: the universe had a beginning
explanations.definition: About 13.8 billion years ago, everything in the universe we can see was packed close together and very hot. It has been stretching and cooling ever since. This is called the Big Bang.
explanations.description: If galaxies are moving apart now, they were closer together in the past. Run the film backwards, and everything was once packed together. Packed things get hot, so the early universe was extremely hot. As it stretched, it cooled. Atoms formed, then stars and galaxies, and much later the Sun, the Earth and us. The Big Bang was not a bomb going off at one spot. It happened everywhere at once, including the place where you are now. Three clues tell us it really happened. Galaxies are moving apart. A faint glow, left over from the hot early universe, comes from every direction in the sky. And the universe is mostly hydrogen and helium, in just the amounts that a hot beginning would make.
examples: Fred Hoyle, an astronomer who did not believe in a beginning, made up the name 'Big Bang' on BBC radio in 1949.
The leftover glow was found in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson. At first they thought the hiss came from pigeon droppings inside their antenna. They cleaned the antenna, and the hiss stayed.
explanations.art: A long strip from left to right: a white-hot glow, then a dark sky with the first small galaxies, then big spiral galaxies, then our Sun and Earth.
explanations.context: This card explains what the Big Bang was, and how we know.

explanations.concept: Looking far is looking back in time
explanations.definition: Light takes time to travel. So we see every faraway thing as it was when its light set off, not as it is now.
explanations.description: Light is the fastest thing there is. It travels about 300,000 kilometres every second. Even so, space is so big that light from far away takes a very long time to reach us. Light from the Moon takes just over 1 second. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes. Light from the Andromeda galaxy takes about 2.5 million years. So when you see Andromeda, you see it as it was before there were any people like us on Earth. The further away a galaxy is, the older the picture we see. This lets astronomers look back at the young universe. The Webb space telescope has seen galaxies whose light set off more than 13 billion years ago, when the universe was very young.
examples: India's AstroSat space telescope picked up ultraviolet light from a galaxy called AUDFs01, about 9.3 billion light-years away. The team was led by Kanak Saha in Pune, and they reported it in 2020.
Light from the middle of the Milky Way set off about 26,000 years ago.
explanations.art: A child looking through a telescope at a galaxy, with a long dotted line of light from the galaxy to the child, and a calendar at the galaxy's end showing a date millions of years ago.
explanations.context: This card explains why far light is old light.

explanations.concept: How astronomers measure how far a galaxy is
explanations.definition: A star that really shines brightly looks faint when it is far away. If you know how bright a star really is, how faint it looks tells you how far away it is.
explanations.description: A torch close to you looks bright. The same torch at the end of a long road looks dim. If you know it is the same torch, you can tell how far away it is from how dim it looks. Henrietta Leavitt found a kind of star that works like this. Cepheid stars get brighter and dimmer in a steady rhythm. In 1912 she showed that the slower a Cepheid blinks, the brighter it really is. So astronomers time a Cepheid's blinks, work out how bright it really is, and compare that with how bright it looks.
examples: Edwin Hubble timed a Cepheid in Andromeda in 1923. It blinked every 31 days but looked very faint, so Andromeda had to be far outside the Milky Way.
For galaxies too far to see a single Cepheid, astronomers use exploding stars called supernovae, which are much brighter.
explanations.art: The same lamp drawn near a child and far down a long road, looking bright and then dim.
explanations.context: This card explains how we know how far away galaxies are.

explanations.concept: What came before the Big Bang?
explanations.description: Nobody knows. Science can follow the universe back to when it was extremely hot and packed together. Before that, our best theories stop working, so we only have ideas. Some scientists think time itself began with the Big Bang, so there was no 'before'. Others think there was something earlier, perhaps another universe that came before ours. None of these ideas has been tested yet.
examples: Stephen Hawking said asking what came before the Big Bang may be like asking what is north of the North Pole.
Roger Penrose thinks our universe may be one in a long chain of universes, one after another.
explanations.art: A timeline of the universe that fades into a question mark at its left end.
explanations.context: This card is about a question nobody can answer yet.

agreed.text: The universe is expanding. Distant galaxies are moving apart, and the further away they are, the faster they move away.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers measure the redshift of galaxies, how much their light is stretched. Since Hubble's work in 1929, thousands of galaxies have been measured, and the further away they are, the more their light is stretched.

agreed.text: About 13.8 billion years ago, the universe was extremely hot and packed together. This is the Big Bang.
agreed.evidence: The expansion, the faint leftover glow found in 1965, and the amounts of hydrogen and helium in the universe all point to the same hot beginning. The Planck spacecraft measured the glow in detail and gives the age as 13.8 billion years.

agreed.text: The Milky Way is one galaxy among hundreds of billions.
agreed.evidence: In 1923, Hubble measured the distance to Andromeda using a Cepheid star, and showed it is far outside the Milky Way. Telescopes such as Hubble and Webb have since photographed tiny patches of sky holding thousands of galaxies.

agreed.text: We see far galaxies as they were in the past.
agreed.evidence: Light travels at a fixed speed, about 300,000 kilometres a second, so it takes time to cross space. The most distant galaxies look smaller, younger and more broken up than nearby ones, which is what we would expect if we see them when the universe was young.

challenging.claim: The Milky Way is the whole universe. The spiral smudges seen in telescopes are small clouds of gas inside it.
challenging.who: Harlow Shapley and many astronomers, in a famous debate with Heber Curtis in 1920
challenging.for: Nobody could measure how far the spiral smudges were. The Milky Way seemed huge, and one astronomer, Adriaan van Maanen, wrongly claimed he had seen the smudges spin, which would mean they were small and close.
challenging.against: In 1923, Hubble found a Cepheid star in Andromeda and showed it is far outside the Milky Way. Van Maanen's measurements turned out to be mistakes.
challenging.context: This card is about an idea most astronomers held about a hundred years ago.

challenging.claim: The universe has always existed and looks the same at all times. As galaxies move apart, new matter quietly appears to fill the gaps. This is called the steady state theory.
challenging.who: Fred Hoyle, Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold, from 1948
challenging.for: It explained why galaxies move apart without needing a beginning. Many people found a universe with no beginning easier to accept.
challenging.against: In 1965 Penzias and Wilson found the faint glow left from a hot early universe. A steady state universe would have no such glow. Far galaxies, seen as they were long ago, also look different from nearby ones.
challenging.context: This card is about an idea that competed with the Big Bang.

challenging.claim: The Big Bang was an explosion at one spot in space, and the galaxies are flying away from that spot.
challenging.who: Many people, because of the name 'Big Bang'
challenging.for: The name sounds like an explosion, and galaxies are moving apart, like pieces after a blast.
challenging.against: If galaxies were flying from one spot, there would be a centre, and galaxies there would see things differently from galaxies at the edge. Astronomers see the same pattern in every direction. The stretching happens everywhere at once.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake about the Big Bang.

challenging.claim: The two main ways of measuring how fast the universe expands give different answers, so something may be missing from our picture of the universe.
challenging.who: Many astronomers, including Adam Riess and his team
challenging.for: Measuring nearby galaxies with Cepheids and exploding stars gives a faster speed than working it out from the leftover glow. Both sets of measurements have been checked many times.
challenging.against: Some astronomers think a small mistake in one of the methods will explain the difference, and newer measurements sometimes come out closer together.
challenging.context: This card is about a puzzle astronomers are working on right now.

big_questions.q: Every bindi on the balloon saw the others move away. If every place is like that, where is the centre of the universe?
big_questions.hint: Think about the balloon. Could you point to the centre on its skin? Is the middle of the air inside part of the model?

big_questions.q: When you see the Andromeda galaxy, are you seeing Andromeda, or a message that Andromeda sent long ago?
big_questions.hint: The light set off 2.5 million years ago. What has reached your eye: the galaxy, or its light?

big_questions.q: Can something begin from nothing? What would 'nothing' be?
big_questions.hint: Try to imagine nothing at all: no space, no time, no dark. Is it even possible to picture?

big_questions.q: If the universe began 13.8 billion years ago, did time begin then too?
big_questions.hint: Some scientists say yes and some say no. What would 'before time' mean?

big_questions.q: Somewhere in a far galaxy, someone may be looking at the Milky Way. What would they see of us?
big_questions.hint: Our light takes millions or billions of years to reach them. What was the Earth like that long ago?

big_questions.q: We are made of atoms from the early universe and from old stars. Is the universe looking at itself through your eyes?
big_questions.hint: Where did the hydrogen in your body come from? Where did the carbon come from?

story.title: The Smudge over the Javadi Hills
story.note: Kavya, Arjun, Periamma Meenakshi and their family are made up. The Javadi Hills in Tamil Nadu are real. The Vainu Bappu Observatory at Kavalur was built there because the skies are dark. The way to find Andromeda in the story is the usual one: from the corner of the Great Square of Pegasus, two stars along, then up. Andromeda can be seen with the eyes alone only from a dark place, on evenings from about October to January. For the parent: Kavya learns that the faint smudge is a whole galaxy, and that its light is so old that she is seeing the galaxy's past. Then she uses a balloon to show her father that galaxies moving away from us does not put us at the centre.
text: In the Deepavali holidays, Kavya and her little brother Arjun went to stay with their Periamma, their mother's elder sister, in the Javadi Hills. Periamma Meenakshi was an astronomer. The village was small, and at night the only lights were a few lamps in windows. Above the hills, the sky was crowded with stars.

On the second night, Periamma spread a mat on the flat roof. Appa came up too, carrying a flask of hot coffee. 'Tonight I want to show you something very far away,' said Periamma. 'First, let your eyes get used to the dark. No phones.'

They lay on the mat and waited. Arjun counted stars and lost count. After a while, Periamma pointed high up towards the north-east. 'Do you see a big square of four stars? Like a box with no lid?' Kavya found it. 'Now go to the corner on the left. From there, follow a line of two bright stars further along. At the second one, turn and look up a little. Look slightly to one side of the spot, not straight at it.'
Kavya looked, and looked to the side, and there it was. A faint grey smudge, like a thumbprint on a window. 'It's a tiny cloud,' said Arjun.

'Watch it,' said Periamma. 'Does it blow away like a cloud?' They watched. Real clouds drifted past and went. The smudge stayed in its place among the stars. 'That is the Andromeda galaxy,' said Periamma. 'It is not a cloud, and it is not one star. It is a whole galaxy, a giant group of about a trillion stars. It is the furthest thing you can see with your eyes alone.'
'A trillion stars, and it looks like a smudge?' said Kavya.

'It is very far away,' said Periamma. 'So far that its light takes about two and a half million years to reach us. The light going into your eye right now set off from Andromeda two and a half million years ago.'
Kavya thought about this. 'Were there people then?'

'Not people like us,' said Periamma. 'There were early relatives of humans in Africa, and some were starting to make stone tools. When that light set off, nobody on Earth could have looked up and wondered about it. It has been travelling all that time, and tonight it has landed in your eye.'
'So I'm not seeing Andromeda now,' said Kavya slowly. 'I'm seeing it as it was, a very long time ago.'

'Yes,' said Periamma. 'Every time you look far, you look back in time. The Moon you see is just over one second old. The Sun is about eight minutes old. Andromeda is two and a half million years old. The furthest galaxies that big telescopes see are pictures from when the universe was very young.'
Appa poured the coffee. 'I read that all the galaxies are rushing away from us,' he said. 'So we must be right in the middle of everything. That makes us quite special.'

'Andromeda is one of the few coming closer,' said Periamma. 'Gravity pulls our two galaxies together. But it is true that almost all the far galaxies are moving away from us, and the further they are, the faster they go.' She smiled at Kavya. 'Is your Appa right? Are we in the middle?'
Kavya did not know. She lay awake for a long time that night, thinking about it.

The next morning there was a village fair, and Arjun came home with a red balloon. Kavya had an idea. She borrowed Amma's packet of bindis and stuck six of them on the balloon, while it was still small. She called one of them 'Milky Way'.
'Appa, blow it up, please,' she said. Appa blew. The balloon grew, and the bindis spread apart. 'Look at Milky Way,' said Kavya. 'All the other bindis moved away from it. The far ones moved most.'
'So Milky Way is the centre,' said Appa.

'Now look from this one,' said Kavya, and put her finger on a different bindi. 'All the others moved away from this one too. And from this one. Every bindi sees the others go away. None of them is the centre.'
Appa turned the balloon round and round in his hands. 'So if I lived on any of these bindis, I would think I was in the middle,' he said. 'And so would everyone else.'
'And look,' said Kavya. 'The bindis didn't get bigger. Only the rubber between them stretched. Periamma says galaxies don't stretch either. It's the space between them.'
Periamma had been listening from the doorway. 'That is exactly what astronomers found,' she said. 'Your Appa's idea was what many people thought at first. You have just shown him why it isn't so.'

That night, Kavya went up to the roof again. She found the square, the corner, the two stars, and the faint smudge. Somewhere in that smudge, she thought, there might be someone looking back at the Milky Way. And from there, our galaxy would seem to be in the middle too.
story.epiphany: Kavya realises two things. The faint smudge of Andromeda is a whole galaxy, and because its light is so old, she is seeing its past, not its present. And galaxies moving away from us does not put us at the centre, because from every bindi on her balloon, the others moved away.
ask: Why did Periamma tell Kavya to look slightly to one side of the smudge?
How did they know the smudge was not a cloud?
Kavya said she was not seeing Andromeda now. What did she mean?
Appa thought we must be in the middle of everything. How did Kavya show him what the balloon says?
Why didn't the bindis get bigger when the balloon grew? What does that tell us about galaxies?

games.title: Old Light: a galaxy card game
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is the Old Light card game. Each card is a real galaxy. The galaxy whose light set off longest ago wins the round.

printables.title: 12 galaxy cards, each with a name, a shape and when its light set off
items: THE MILKY WAY. Barred spiral. We live inside it. Light from its centre set off about 26,000 years ago.
LARGE MAGELLANIC CLOUD. Irregular. A small galaxy close to ours. Its light set off about 160,000 years ago.
SMALL MAGELLANIC CLOUD. Irregular. Another small galaxy close to ours. Its light set off about 200,000 years ago.
ANDROMEDA. Spiral, seen at a slant. Our nearest big neighbour. Its light set off about 2.5 million years ago.
THE CIGAR GALAXY (M82). Irregular, making new stars very fast. Its light set off about 12 million years ago.
THE PINWHEEL (M101). Spiral, seen from the top. Its light set off about 21 million years ago.
THE SOMBRERO (M104). Spiral, seen almost from the side. Its light set off about 28 million years ago.
THE WHIRLPOOL (M51). Spiral, with a small galaxy passing close. Its light set off about 31 million years ago.
M87. Giant elliptical, with a huge black hole in the middle. Its light set off about 55 million years ago.
THE CARTWHEEL. A ring-shaped galaxy, hit by a smaller galaxy. Its light set off about 500 million years ago.
AUDFs01. Small and faint, seen by India's AstroSat. Its light set off about 9.3 billion years ago.
JADES-GS-z14-0. A tiny young galaxy seen by the Webb telescope. Its light set off about 13.5 billion years ago.

printables.title: A score sheet with a column for each player, and a row for each round

rules: Shuffle the 12 galaxy cards and deal them out equally, face down.
Each round, every player turns over their top card and reads it out.
The card whose light set off longest ago wins. That galaxy is the furthest away, so we are seeing the oldest picture.
The winner keeps all the cards from that round.
Bonus round: if two cards show the same shape, the first player to call out the shape wins both cards.
When all the cards are played, the player with the most cards wins.

flow.do: 1. Shuffle and deal the cards. 2. Explain how a round is won.
flow.say: Each card is a real galaxy. The one whose light set off longest ago wins, because its picture is the oldest.
flow.kid: Each card is a real galaxy. The oldest light wins the round.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Old Light game.

flow.do: Play the first round together as practice, with the Andromeda card and the Pinwheel card.
flow.say: Andromeda's light set off 2.5 million years ago. The Pinwheel's set off 21 million years ago. Which wins?
flow.kid: Andromeda, 2.5 million years. Pinwheel, 21 million years. Which light is older?

check.q: Which galaxy's light is older, so that galaxy is further away?
check.why: 21 million years is longer than 2.5 million years. The Pinwheel's light has travelled longer, so the Pinwheel is further away, and we see an older picture of it.

flow.do: Play the game until all the cards are used.
flow.say: Your turn. Read your card out loud, then let's see whose light is oldest.
flow.kid: Read your card out loud. Whose light is oldest?
flow.parent: Help with the big numbers. A billion is a thousand million, so 9.3 billion years beats 500 million years.

flow.do: Look at the winning card from the last round and talk about it.
flow.say: The JADES card's light set off 13.5 billion years ago. The universe is 13.8 billion years old. How young was the universe when that light set off?
flow.kid: How young was the universe when the JADES light set off?

ask.q: How old was the universe when that light set off?
good: About 300 million years old.
Very young: 13.8 take away 13.5 is 0.3 billion.

experiments.title: The Bindi Balloon: do far bindis move away faster than near ones?
experiments.question: When a balloon grows, do the bindis on it all move apart by the same amount? Is there any bindi that the others do not move away from?
experiments.predict: Before you blow the balloon bigger, guess. Will a near bindi and a far bindi move away from your home bindi by the same amount, or different amounts? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use one balloon and do not move the bindis. Measure every gap the same way, from the middle of one bindi to the middle of the other, with the thread lying flat on the rubber. Measure all the gaps when the balloon is small, then all of them again when it is big.

materials.item: a round balloon, light-coloured if you have one
6 stick-on bindis, of different colours or sizes so you can tell them apart (or small dots of paper stuck on with a tiny piece of cellotape)
a piece of sewing thread, about 40 cm long
a 30 cm ruler
a cloth peg or a hair clip, to hold the balloon's neck shut
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up blows up the balloon. Stop before the rubber gets tight, so it does not burst near anyone's face. If it bursts, pick up every piece at once. Balloon pieces can choke a child, so they never go in the mouth.

schedule.what: Guess. Stick six bindis on a small balloon. Measure the gaps. Blow it bigger. Measure again. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then write one sentence: the bindi that was furthest away moved ____ cm, and the nearest one moved ____ cm.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the balloon and the bindis. 2. Ask the guess question below. 3. Wait for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Each bindi will be a galaxy, and the balloon's rubber will be space. When I blow the balloon bigger, will a near bindi and a far bindi move away by the same amount? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Each bindi is a galaxy. The rubber is space. When the balloon grows, will near and far bindis move the same? Guess. Say why.

ask.q: Which bindi do you think will move furthest from home? Why?
good: They will all move the same, because the balloon grows the same everywhere.
The far one, because there is more rubber between them to stretch.

flow.parent: Accept any guess with a reason. Do not give the answer. The measuring will show it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bindi Balloon experiment. You find out how things move apart when the space between them grows.

flow.do: 1. Blow the balloon up to about the size of a big mango, around 12 cm across. 2. Twist the neck and clip it with the peg. 3. Your child sticks the home bindi in the middle of the fat part. 4. They stick three more in a rough line from it, about 3 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm away. 5. They stick the last two anywhere else.
flow.say: This first bindi is our home, the Milky Way. Now stick three in a line going away from it, a little further each time. Put the last two anywhere.
flow.kid: Stick the home bindi in the middle. Stick three more in a line, each one further away. Put two more anywhere.
flow.parent: Keep the bindis on the fat middle of the balloon, away from the neck, because the rubber near the neck stretches less. Give each bindi a letter on the results table: H for home, then A, B and C along the line, and D and E for the other two.
flow.context: In this step of the Bindi Balloon experiment, you set up the small balloon.

flow.do: 1. Hold one end of the thread on the middle of H. 2. Lay the thread flat along the rubber to the middle of A. 3. Pinch the thread there, lift it off, and hold it against the ruler. 4. Write the gap in the table. 5. Do the same for H to B, H to C, C to A and C to B.
flow.say: Hold the thread on the home bindi. Lay it along the rubber to the next one, and pinch it there. Now let's read it on the ruler.
flow.kid: Hold the thread on H. Lay it to A. Pinch it. Read it on the ruler. Write it down.
flow.parent: This needs two pairs of hands: one person holds the thread end on the bindi, the other lays it and pinches. Round each gap to the nearest half centimetre. The gaps from C let you look at the balloon from a second bindi later.
flow.context: In this step of the Bindi Balloon experiment, you measure the gaps on the small balloon.

flow.do: 1. Unclip the neck, holding it tight. 2. Blow the balloon bigger, to about twice as wide, around 24 cm across. 3. Clip it shut again.
flow.say: Watch the bindis while I blow. What do you see them doing?
flow.kid: Watch the bindis while the balloon grows. What are they doing?

ask.q: What did you see while the balloon grew?
good: All the bindis spread apart.
The far ones seemed to move faster.

flow.parent: Stop before the rubber feels tight. A balloon that is nearly full is more likely to burst.

flow.do: 1. Measure the same five gaps again, in the same way. 2. Write them in the table. 3. For each pair, take the small gap from the big gap and write how much further apart they are.
flow.say: Let's measure the same gaps again. Then we can work out how much further apart each pair has gone.
flow.kid: Measure the same gaps again. Write them down. How much further apart is each pair?

check.q: From home, which bindi moved furthest away?
check.why: C started furthest away, so there was the most rubber between H and C to stretch. If the balloon doubled in width, a 3 cm gap became about 6 cm, but a 9 cm gap became about 18 cm. If your numbers show something else, check that every bindi is on the fat middle of the balloon.

flow.do: 1. Look at the gaps measured from C. 2. Ask: did the other bindis move away from C as well? 3. Measure one bindi across its middle with the ruler, and compare it with how big it was before.
flow.say: Now pretend C is home. Did the other bindis move away from C too? And did the bindis themselves get any bigger?
flow.kid: Pretend C is home. Did the others move away from C too? Did the bindis get bigger?

ask.q: Was there any bindi that the others did not move away from?
good: No. From every bindi, the others moved away.
None of them is the middle.

flow.parent: The bindis stay the same size because they are stuck on, and only the rubber between them stretches. Galaxies are like this: gravity holds them together, and only the space between them grows. Only the balloon's skin stands for space. The air inside and the room outside are not part of the model.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why does it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: when space stretches, far things move apart faster than near things, and there is no centre. What I saw: the bindi 9 cm away moved about three times as far as the one 3 cm away, and the bindis moved away from C as well as from H. Why: there is more rubber between far bindis, so more of it stretches. Now explain: galaxies are moving away from us in the same way. Hubble found that a galaxy twice as far away moves away about twice as fast. Every galaxy would see the same thing, so we are not at the centre.

experiments.title: Tilt the Spiral: can one galaxy look like different shapes?
experiments.question: Does a spiral galaxy look the same from every direction? Does a ball-shaped galaxy?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When you hold the plate so you see it exactly from the side, what shape will the spiral make? Will the orange change shape when you turn it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Look at both models from the same distance, about one big step away, with one eye closed. Change only one thing: how much the model is tilted. Use the same three tilts for both: from the top, at a slant, and from the side.
results_table: From the top: shape I saw
At a slant: shape I saw
From the side: shape I saw

materials.item: a paper plate, or a circle cut from a cardboard box by drawing round a steel plate
a sketch pen or a dark pencil
a small ball of atta dough or clay, about the size of a grape
an orange, a mosambi or any round ball
paper and a pencil for drawing what you see

experiments.safety: If you cut a circle from a box, a grown-up does the cutting.

schedule.what: Guess. Draw a spiral on a plate. Look at the plate and an orange from the top, at a slant and from the side. Draw each shape. Compare with real galaxy photos.

experiments.record: Draw the six shapes you saw in the results table. Then write which model changed shape and which did not.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the four galaxy pictures in the app. 2. Ask the guess question below. 3. Wait for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: A spiral galaxy is a flat spinning disc. What shape would it look like if we saw it from the side? Would a ball of stars change shape? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A spiral galaxy is a flat disc. What would it look like from the side? Guess. Say why.

ask.q: What will the disc look like from the side?
good: Still round, because it is a circle.
A thin line, because it is flat.

flow.parent: Accept any guess with a reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tilt the Spiral experiment. You find out whether a galaxy's shape depends on the direction we see it from.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a spiral with two arms on the plate, starting from the middle. 2. They press the ball of dough onto the middle of the plate. 3. They draw the same spiral on the back.
flow.say: Draw two arms curling out from the middle. Then press the dough in the middle. That is the bulge, where old stars crowd together.
flow.kid: Draw two curly arms from the middle. Press the dough in the middle. That is the bulge.
flow.parent: Real spiral galaxies have a bulge on both sides of the disc. If the dough will not stay, use a bottle cap stuck on with tape.

flow.do: 1. Stand one big step away from your child. 2. Hold the plate flat facing them. 3. Then tilt it halfway. 4. Then turn it until they see only its edge, at the height of their eyes. 5. At each tilt, your child closes one eye and draws what they see.
flow.say: Close one eye. Draw what you see. Now I'll tilt it. Draw again. Now I'll turn it right round to the side.
flow.kid: Close one eye. Draw the plate. Draw it again when it tilts. Draw it from the side.

check.q: What did the plate look like from the side?
options: A thin line with a bump in the middle
check.why: From the side, a flat disc shows only its edge, and the dough bulge sticks up in the middle. The arms are hidden. If you still saw arms, the plate was not turned all the way to the side.

flow.do: Do the same with the orange. Hold it in the same three ways, and your child draws it each time.
flow.say: Now the orange. Watch it from the top, at a slant, and from the side. Does its shape change?
flow.kid: Now look at the orange the same three ways. Draw it. Does its shape change?

ask.q: What happened to the orange's shape?
good: It stayed round every time.
A ball looks round from every side.

flow.do: 1. Show the three real galaxy photos in the app: the Pinwheel, Andromeda and the Sombrero. 2. Ask your child to match each to one of their plate drawings.
flow.say: These are three real spiral galaxies. Which of your drawings looks like each one?
flow.kid: Look at three real spiral galaxies. Which drawing matches each one?
flow.parent: The Pinwheel is seen from the top, Andromeda at a slant, and the Sombrero almost from the side. All three are spiral galaxies. They only look different because of the direction we see them from.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why does it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a spiral galaxy looks round, oval or like a line, depending on where we see it from, but a ball of stars looks round from everywhere. What I saw: the plate changed from a circle to a thin line, but the orange stayed round. Why: the plate is flat and the orange is not. Now explain: astronomers can only photograph each galaxy from one direction, from Earth. So they look for clues, like a bulge or a dark line of dust, to tell a disc seen from the side from a different kind of galaxy.

activities.title: First Look: four galaxies, four shapes

materials.item: the four galaxy pictures in the app: the Pinwheel, the Sombrero, M87 and the Large Magellanic Cloud
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Look at four galaxies. Say what you notice and what you wonder. Sort them by shape.

activities.record: Draw the four galaxies quickly, and write one thing you wonder about them.

flow.do: 1. Show the four pictures. Do not say what they are yet. 2. Ask what your child notices, and what they wonder.
flow.say: Look at these four pictures. What do you notice about them? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look at the four pictures. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

good: One has curly arms.
One is a smooth oval.
One has no shape at all.
They are all made of lots of dots of light.

flow.parent: Write down what your child wonders. The rest of the unit may answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the First Look activity. You look at four real galaxies before learning about them.

flow.do: Tell your child what the pictures are. Each one is a whole galaxy, made of billions of stars.
flow.say: Each of these is a galaxy, a huge group of billions of stars. Each little dot of light you see is many stars together. Our Sun lives in a galaxy too, called the Milky Way.
flow.kid: Each picture is a galaxy. A galaxy is billions of stars together. Our Sun is in one too.
flow.parent: The Pinwheel is a spiral seen from the top. The Sombrero is a spiral seen nearly from the side. M87 is a giant elliptical galaxy. The Large Magellanic Cloud is a small irregular galaxy.

flow.do: Ask your child to sort the four into groups by shape, and give each group a name.
flow.say: Put them into groups by their shape. What would you call each group?
flow.kid: Sort them by shape. Give each group a name.

check.q: Which picture has no clear shape?
check.why: The Large Magellanic Cloud is an irregular galaxy, with no clear shape. The Pinwheel has spiral arms, and M87 is a smooth oval.

activities.title: The Universe in One Year: a calendar on the wall

materials.item: an old wall calendar, or 12 sheets of paper with a month written on each
small slips of paper, sketch pens and cellotape

schedule.what: Squeeze the whole history of the universe into one year. Stick each big event on its date.

activities.record: The calendar on the wall, with each event on its date, and a picture for each.

flow.do: 1. Lay out or hang the 12 months in a row. 2. Explain the rule: the whole 13.8 billion years is squeezed into one year.
flow.say: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. Let's squeeze all of it into one year. The Big Bang is the first moment of 1 January. Today is the last moment of 31 December. Each day stands for about 38 million years.
flow.kid: Squeeze the universe's whole life into one year. The Big Bang is 1 January. Now is midnight on 31 December.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Universe in One Year activity. You make the universe's long history small enough to see.

flow.do: Your child writes each event on a slip and sticks it on its date. Read out the dates from the note.
flow.say: Before we stick each one, guess. When in the year do you think the Sun and the Earth were made?
flow.kid: Guess when each thing happened. Then stick it on its date.

ask.q: When do you think the Sun and Earth were made?
good: In January, near the start.
Halfway through the year.

flow.parent: Dates on the one-year calendar: 1 January, the Big Bang. About 9 January, the light set off from the furthest galaxies the Webb telescope has seen. January and February, the Milky Way's oldest stars form. About 1 September, the Sun and Earth form. Late September, the first living things on Earth. 30 December, the dinosaurs die out. 31 December at about 10:25 at night, the light we see tonight sets off from Andromeda. 31 December at about 11:48 at night, the first modern humans.

flow.do: Look at the calendar together. Point at where all of human history fits.
flow.say: Look how empty most of the year is for us. All of human history fits into the last few minutes of 31 December. Your whole life is less than one fiftieth of a second.
flow.kid: All of human history is in the last minutes of the year. Your life is less than a blink.

check.q: On the one-year calendar, when did the light we see from Andromeda set off?
check.why: Andromeda's light set off 2.5 million years ago. One day on the calendar is about 38 million years, so 2.5 million years is less than one day. That puts it late on 31 December, about an hour and a half before midnight.

flow.do: Your child draws a small picture next to each event.
flow.say: Draw a little picture for each one. What would the universe have looked like on 9 January?
flow.kid: Draw a small picture for each event.
flow.parent: On 9 January the universe was full of small, young galaxies, and there was no Sun or Earth yet.

activities.title: Stretch the Elastic: does every mark move the same?

materials.item: a piece of flat elastic, about 30 cm long, from a tailor's shop or an old pyjama (or a big rubber band cut open)
a sketch pen, a ruler and cellotape

activities.safety: Hold the elastic firmly. Do not let it snap back towards anyone's face.

schedule.what: Mark dots on elastic. Stretch it to twice its length. Measure how far each dot moved.

activities.record: A table with each mark's place before and after stretching, and how far it moved.

flow.do: 1. Lay the elastic along the ruler without stretching it. 2. Your child marks dots at 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm. 3. Tape the end with the 0 dot to the table, at 0 on the ruler.
flow.say: These dots are galaxies on a line, 2 centimetres apart. The dot at 0 is home. Let's tape it down.
flow.kid: Mark dots at 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm. The 0 dot is home. Tape it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Stretch the Elastic activity. You test the bindi balloon's pattern again on a straight line.

flow.do: 1. Ask the guess question below. 2. Stretch the elastic along the ruler until the 8 cm dot reaches 16 cm. 3. Hold it there while your child reads where each dot is now.
flow.say: If I stretch it until the last dot reaches 16, where will the dot that was at 2 be? Guess first, and say why.
flow.kid: Guess where each dot will go. Then read the ruler.

ask.q: Where did the dots end up?
good: Every dot doubled its distance from home.

flow.parent: If the elastic is even, the dots land near 4, 8, 12 and 16 cm. Cheap elastic may stretch a little unevenly. Close is good enough.

flow.do: Work out together how far each dot moved, and what pattern you see.
flow.say: The dot at 2 moved 2 centimetres. How far did the dot at 6 move? What is the pattern?
flow.kid: How far did each dot move? Find the pattern.

check.q: The dot that started at 6 cm ended at 12 cm. How far did it move?
check.why: 12 take away 6 is 6. Every dot moved as far as it started from home, because each one's distance doubled. A dot three times as far away moved three times as far, just like the far galaxies Hubble measured.

activities.title: Find Andromeda, if you can get to a dark place

materials.item: a clear night far from city lights, for example in a village or a hill station, from October to January
a mat to lie on, and binoculars if you have them
a torch covered with red cellophane or a red sweet wrapper

activities.safety: A grown-up stays with the child at night. Keep away from the edge of any roof without a wall.

schedule.what: On a dark night, let your eyes get used to the dark, then find the faint smudge of the Andromeda galaxy.

activities.record: A drawing of the Great Square and the smudge, with the date, the time and the place.

flow.do: 1. Around 8 to 9 in the evening, lie on the mat with all lights off. 2. Wait 15 minutes without looking at any screen or white light.
flow.say: Our eyes need time to see faint things. Let's lie here quietly and wait. No phones, no white lights.
flow.kid: Lie still in the dark. Wait 15 minutes. No phones.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Find Andromeda activity. You look for the furthest thing you can see with your eyes alone.

flow.do: 1. Find the Great Square: four stars making a big box, high in the north-east. 2. From its left corner, follow a line of two bright stars. 3. At the second one, look a little upwards for a faint smudge. 4. Look slightly to one side of it.
flow.say: Find the big square of four stars. Go to the left corner, then two stars along. Now look up a little, slightly to one side.
flow.kid: Find the big square. Go to its corner. Two stars along, then look up a bit.
flow.parent: The edge of your eye sees faint things better than the middle, which is why looking slightly to one side helps. With binoculars, the smudge is much easier. If you cannot see it, the sky is not dark enough. Use Stellarium Web to see where it should be.
flow.wait: Do this on a clear, dark night in a place far from city lights.

flow.do: Talk about what you saw.
flow.say: That smudge is a whole galaxy of about a trillion stars. Its light set off two and a half million years ago. What was the Earth like then?
flow.kid: That smudge is a galaxy. Its light is two and a half million years old.

ask.q: Are we seeing Andromeda as it is tonight?
good: No, as it was 2.5 million years ago.
We see its old light.

activities.title: Be a Galaxy Zoo sorter: help real astronomers

materials.item: a phone, tablet or computer, with a grown-up
paper and a pencil for a tally

activities.safety: A grown-up opens the website and stays with the child.

schedule.what: Sort 20 real galaxy photos on the Galaxy Zoo website, and keep a tally of their shapes.

activities.record: A tally of the shapes you sorted, and a bar chart made from it.

flow.do: 1. Open the Galaxy Zoo project on the Zooniverse website. 2. Read the short help with your child.
flow.say: Real astronomers have far more galaxy photos than they can look at. Volunteers all over the world help sort them. We can help too.
flow.kid: Astronomers have too many galaxy photos. You can help sort them.
flow.parent: Galaxy Zoo began in 2007. In its first year, a Dutch schoolteacher called Hanny van Arkel spotted a strange glowing green cloud that no astronomer had noticed. It is now called Hanny's Voorwerp, which is Dutch for Hanny's object.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Galaxy Zoo activity. You sort real galaxy photos for a science project.

flow.do: Your child answers the questions for 20 galaxies. For each one, they also make a tally mark: spiral, smooth, or something else.
flow.say: Is this one smooth and round, or does it have arms or a disc? Make a tally mark too.
flow.kid: Smooth, or arms and a disc? Answer. Then make a tally mark.

flow.do: Count the tally marks together.
flow.say: Which shape did we see most? Why might that be?
flow.kid: Count your tally. Which shape did you see most?

ask.q: Why might some photos be hard to sort?
good: Some are blurry because they are so far away.
Some spirals are seen from the side, so you can't see the arms.

projects.title: My Galaxy Field Guide

materials.item: 6 sheets of paper, folded and stapled into a small book
colour pencils or crayons
galaxy photos from the ESA/Hubble or Webb websites, looked at with a grown-up

projects.safety: A grown-up chooses the websites and stays with the child online.

schedule.what: Make the book. Draw and describe a spiral and a barred spiral galaxy, one on each page.
Draw and describe an elliptical and an irregular galaxy.
Add a page on our own galaxy, and a page on 'how to tell which shape it is'.

projects.record: The finished field guide, with one galaxy shape per page.

flow.do: 1. Fold and staple the book. 2. Your child picks a real spiral galaxy and a real barred spiral. 3. On each page, they draw it and write its name, its shape and when its light set off.
flow.say: A field guide helps people tell things apart. Draw this galaxy and write three things: its name, its shape and how old its light is.
flow.kid: Draw a galaxy. Write its name, its shape and how old its light is.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Galaxy Field Guide project. You make your own book of galaxy shapes.

flow.do: Your child adds an elliptical galaxy and an irregular galaxy, in the same way.
flow.say: Now an elliptical and an irregular galaxy. What makes each one different from a spiral?
flow.kid: Add an elliptical and an irregular galaxy. How are they different?

flow.do: 1. Your child adds a page about the Milky Way. 2. They add a last page of tips for telling galaxy shapes apart.
flow.say: What tips would you give someone sorting galaxies? Remember the plate and the orange.
flow.kid: Write tips for telling galaxy shapes apart. Remember the plate and the orange.

good: A spiral seen from the side looks like a thin line, so look for a bulge.
Blue patches mean new stars, so it might be a spiral or irregular.
