opts: Our galaxy, the one our Sun is in
A cloud of milky gas near the Earth
The path of the Moon across the sky
Another name for the Andromeda galaxy
quiz.why: The Milky Way is our galaxy. From a dark place we see part of it as a faint band of light, made of the light of billions of stars.

quiz.p: Which kind of galaxy is a smooth oval of stars, with no arms?
opts: Elliptical
Spiral
Barred spiral
Irregular
quiz.why: Elliptical galaxies are smooth ovals or balls of mostly old stars. Spirals and barred spirals have arms. Irregular galaxies have no clear shape.

quiz.p: In the Bindi Balloon test, Revathi measured the gaps between her bindis before and after blowing the balloon bigger. What did she find?
opts: The far bindis moved further away than the near ones
Only the near bindis moved
All the bindis moved the same amount
The bindis moved closer together
quiz.why: There was more rubber between home and the far bindis, so more of it stretched. If you picked 'all the same amount', try measuring the gaps again.
quiz.context: In the Bindi Balloon experiment, you stick bindis on a small balloon, measure the gaps between them with a thread, blow the balloon bigger, and measure again.

quiz.p: Almost every galaxy is moving away from us. Does that mean we are at the centre of the universe?
opts: Yes, everything moves away from the centre
No, from any galaxy, the others would seem to move away
Yes, because the Milky Way is the biggest galaxy
quiz.why: On the balloon, every bindi saw the others move away. So every galaxy sees the same, and no galaxy is the centre. The Milky Way is not the biggest galaxy either.

quiz.p: Why are galaxies far apart moving away from each other?
opts: The space between them is stretching
They are running away from a giant black hole
A wind in space pushes them
They are falling towards the Sun
quiz.why: The galaxies are not being pushed. The space between them is growing, like the rubber between the bindis.

opts: The time, about 13.8 billion years ago, when the universe was very hot and packed together, before it stretched out
A huge bomb that exploded at one spot in space
The noise a star makes when it explodes
The crash when two galaxies meet
quiz.why: The Big Bang was not an explosion at one spot, and it made no sound. It was the hot, packed start of the universe, which has been stretching and cooling ever since.

quiz.p: Which of these is a clue that the universe had a hot beginning?
opts: A faint glow of microwaves reaches us from every direction
Stars twinkle
The Moon changes shape
Galaxies have different shapes
quiz.why: The faint glow, found in 1965, is light left from when the whole universe was hot. Twinkling comes from our air, and the Moon's shape comes from where it is lit by the Sun.

quiz.p: Light from the Andromeda galaxy set off about 2.5 million years ago. So when you see Andromeda, what are you seeing?
opts: Andromeda as it was 2.5 million years ago
Andromeda as it is tonight
A reflection of the Milky Way
quiz.why: Light takes time to travel, so we always see faraway things as they were when their light set off.

quiz.p: Kavya looks at a galaxy twice as far away as Andromeda. Compared with Andromeda's light, when did her galaxy's light set off?
opts: About twice as long ago
At the same time
More recently
quiz.why: Twice as far means the light took about twice as long to arrive, so it set off about twice as long ago, around 5 million years.

quiz.p: Before 1923, what did many astronomers think the faint spiral smudges in their telescopes were?
opts: Clouds of gas inside our Milky Way
Other galaxies
Planets
Comets
quiz.why: Many thought the Milky Way was the whole universe, and the smudges were clouds inside it. Hubble's measurement of Andromeda in 1923 showed they are other galaxies.

quiz.p: Henrietta Leavitt's discovery let Edwin Hubble measure how far away Andromeda is. What had she found?
opts: How long a blinking star takes to blink tells you how bright it really is
How to build a giant telescope
That Andromeda is coming towards us
quiz.why: Knowing how bright a star really is, and how faint it looks, tells you how far away it is. Hubble used her rule on a blinking star in Andromeda.

quiz.p: What came before the Big Bang?
opts: Nobody knows yet
An earlier universe, for certain
Nothing at all, for certain
A giant star
quiz.why: Scientists have ideas, but none has been tested. Some think time began with the Big Bang. Others think an earlier universe came first.

quiz.p: On her balloon, Sara chose a different bindi to be home and looked at the gaps measured from it. What did she find?
opts: The other bindis moved away from her new home bindi too
Only the first home bindi saw the others move away
The bindis all moved towards her new home bindi
quiz.why: From every bindi, all the others moved away. That is why there is no centre.
quiz.context: In the Bindi Balloon experiment, you stick bindis on a small balloon, measure the gaps between them with a thread, blow the balloon bigger, and measure again.

quiz.p: As the universe stretches, the Earth and your body stretch too.
quiz.why: False. The stretching shows only across the huge gaps between groups of galaxies. Close by, the forces holding things together are far stronger, just as the bindis stayed the same size.

items.p: What is a galaxy?
opts: A huge group of stars, gas and dust, held together by gravity
One very bright star
A cloud in the Earth's air
Another name for the Solar System
items.why: A galaxy holds billions of stars. Picking 'a cloud in the Earth's air' is what a galaxy looks like through a small telescope, which is why people once called them nebulae, the Latin word for clouds.

items.p: The Milky Way is the only galaxy there is.
items.why: False. In 1923 Edwin Hubble showed that Andromeda is a separate galaxy far outside ours. There are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the part of the universe we can see.

items.p: Match each galaxy shape to what it looks like.
pairs: a flat disc with arms that curl out from a bright middle
a disc with a straight bar of stars across the middle, and arms from its ends
a smooth oval or ball of stars, with no arms
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the four main shapes that Edwin Hubble sorted galaxies into in 1926. Our own Milky Way is a barred spiral.

items.p: In the Bindi Balloon test, Divya, a girl in Class 3, stuck three bindis 3 cm, 6 cm and 9 cm from her home bindi. Then she blew the balloon bigger. Which bindi moved furthest from home?
opts: The one that started 3 cm away
The one that started 6 cm away
The one that started 9 cm away
They all moved the same amount
items.why: The bindi that started furthest away moved furthest, because there was the most rubber between it and home to stretch. Picking 'all the same' is the most common first guess, and the measuring shows why it is wrong.
items.context: In the Bindi Balloon experiment, you stick bindis on a small balloon, measure the gaps between them with a thread, blow the balloon bigger, and measure again.

items.p: Light from the Andromeda galaxy takes about ____ million years to reach us.
items.why: Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away, so its light takes about 2.5 million years to get here.

items.p: On your balloon, was there any bindi that the others did not move away from? What does that tell you about where the centre of the universe is?
items.context: In the Bindi Balloon experiment, you stick bindis on a small balloon, measure the gaps between them with a thread, blow the balloon bigger, and measure again.
items.a: No. From every bindi, all the others moved away. So no bindi was the centre. In the same way, from every galaxy the others seem to move away, so there is no centre of the universe that we can find.
items.why: A strong answer uses the measurements from a second bindi, such as C, not only from home.

items.p: Sort these. Is each one a galaxy, or a single star?
items: Sirius, the brightest star at night
items.a: see items
items.why: A galaxy is billions of stars together. The Sun, Sirius and the Pole Star are single stars inside our own galaxy, the Milky Way.

items.p: When you look at a far galaxy, you see it as it is right now.
items.why: False. Its light took a long time to reach you, so you see the galaxy as it was when the light set off.

items.p: Scientists say the universe was very hot and packed together at the start. About how long ago was that?
opts: About 6,000 years ago
About 4.6 billion years ago
About 13.8 billion years ago
Never. It has always been the same.
items.why: About 13.8 billion years ago. If you picked 4.6 billion, that is when the Sun and Earth formed, much later. The idea that the universe has always been the same was the steady state theory, and the leftover glow found in 1965 showed it was wrong.

items.p: Draw a spiral galaxy, an elliptical galaxy and an irregular galaxy. Write the name under each one.
items.a: The spiral has a bright middle and curling arms. The elliptical is a smooth oval with no arms. The irregular is a patchy cloud with no clear shape.
items.why: Drawing them side by side shows how each shape is different.
items.art: Three empty boxes labelled spiral, elliptical and irregular.

items.p: Galaxies far apart are moving away from each other because the ____ between them is stretching.
items.why: The galaxies are not flying away from one spot. The space between them is growing, like the rubber between the bindis.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Spiral
Elliptical
Irregular
Nakshatra
items.why: Spiral, elliptical and irregular are galaxy shapes. A nakshatra is one of the 27 star groups along the Moon's path.

items.p: Ananya, a girl in Class 3, and her family are talking about galaxies moving away from us.

views.says: Almost every galaxy is moving away from us. So we must be at the centre of the universe.
On my balloon, every bindi saw the others move away. So every galaxy would see the same thing, and there is no centre.
We can only see part of the universe. So we can't know where the middle is, or if it has one.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give a reason from the balloon test. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer often agrees with Ananya, using the measurements from a second bindi. It also admits that Thatha's idea is a fair first guess, and that Farhana is right that we see only part of the universe.
items.why: Thatha's idea was what many people thought at first. Ananya's is what astronomers found. Farhana's point is a real limit: light from beyond a certain distance has not had time to reach us.

items.p: Rohini, a girl in Class 4, says the Big Bang was a bomb that went off at one place in space. Use your balloon test to explain what is wrong with her picture.
items.context: In the Bindi Balloon experiment, you stick bindis on a small balloon, measure the gaps between them with a thread, blow the balloon bigger, and measure again.
items.a: A bomb has a centre, and the pieces fly away from that spot. On the balloon, there was no centre. Every bindi moved away from every other one, because the rubber stretched everywhere at once. The Big Bang was space stretching everywhere, not an explosion at one spot.
items.why: A strong answer names what a bomb has (a centre) and what the balloon showed (no centre).

items.p: Why do we see far galaxies as they were long ago?
opts: Their light takes a very long time to reach us
Telescopes only show old photos
Far galaxies are older than near ones
Light gets tired and slows down
items.why: Light travels very fast, but space is so big that light from far galaxies takes millions or billions of years to arrive. Light does not slow down or get tired. Far galaxies are not older. We just see them at an earlier time.

items.p: In the Tilt the Spiral test, the paper plate looked round, then oval, then like a thin line. Why might an astronomer think a spiral galaxy seen from the side is a different kind of galaxy?
items.context: In the Tilt the Spiral experiment, you draw a spiral galaxy on a paper plate, look at it from the top, at a slant and from the side, and do the same with an orange.
items.a: From the side, you cannot see the spiral arms. The galaxy looks like a thin line with a bump, not a spiral. So you could think it is a different shape.
items.why: A strong answer says what is hidden from the side (the arms) and what can still give it away (the bulge or a dark line of dust).

items.p: In the Tilt the Spiral test, Lakshmi turns an orange round in her hand. What shape does she see from every side?
opts: Always a circle
A thin line from the side
An oval from the top
items.why: A ball looks round from every side. Elliptical galaxies are more like balls, so their shape changes little with direction. A disc, like the plate, changes a lot.
items.context: In the Tilt the Spiral experiment, you draw a spiral galaxy on a paper plate, look at it from the top, at a slant and from the side, and do the same with an orange.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one whose light set off most recently to the one whose light set off longest ago.
items: The centre of the Milky Way
The furthest galaxies the Webb telescope has seen
items.a: order shown
items.why: Just over 1 second for the Moon, about 8 minutes for the Sun, about 26,000 years for the Milky Way's centre, about 2.5 million years for Andromeda, and more than 13 billion years for the furthest galaxies.

items.p: A light-year is how far light travels in one ____.
items.why: A light-year is a distance, about 9.5 million million kilometres, even though it has the word 'year' in it.

items.p: Henrietta Leavitt studied stars that get brighter and dimmer again and again. What did she find?
opts: The brighter such a star really is, the slower it blinks
All these stars blink at the same speed
These stars are all inside the Solar System
items.why: In 1912 she showed that brighter Cepheids blink more slowly. So timing the blinks tells you how bright the star really is, and that lets you work out how far away it is.

items.p: In 1923, Edwin Hubble found one of Henrietta Leavitt's blinking stars in the Andromeda 'nebula'. It blinked slowly but looked very faint. Why did that show that Andromeda is not part of the Milky Way?
items.a: A slow blink meant the star was really very bright. But it looked very faint. A very bright star only looks faint if it is very far away. It was much further away than the edge of the Milky Way, so Andromeda had to be a separate galaxy.
items.why: A strong answer links three steps: slow blink, really bright, looks faint, so very far.

items.p: Galaxies themselves are getting bigger as the universe expands.
items.why: False. Gravity holds a galaxy's stars together, so the galaxy does not grow. Only the space between groups of galaxies stretches. On the balloon, the bindis stayed the same size.

items.p: Sort these galaxies by their shape.
items.a: see items
items.why: Andromeda, the Whirlpool and the Pinwheel have spiral arms. M87 is a smooth giant oval. The two Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies with no clear shape.

items.p: In the Stretch the Elastic activity, Meena's marks at 2 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm ended up at 4 cm, 8 cm and 12 cm. How far did the mark that started at 6 cm move?
opts: 2 cm
4 cm
6 cm
12 cm
items.why: It went from 6 cm to 12 cm, so it moved 6 cm. The mark at 2 cm moved only 2 cm. The mark three times as far moved three times as much. If you picked 12 cm, that is where it ended, not how far it moved.
items.context: In the Stretch the Elastic activity, you mark dots 2 centimetres apart on a piece of elastic, tape one end down, and stretch it to twice its length.

items.p: Label the parts of the spiral galaxy on the drawing: the bulge, the disc, a spiral arm, and a place where young blue stars are.
items.a: The bulge is the bright round middle. The disc is the whole flat part. A spiral arm is one of the curling bright bands. Young blue stars are along the arms.
items.why: New stars are made where gas is squeezed together in the arms. The youngest, hottest stars are blue.
items.art: A spiral galaxy drawn face-on with four blank label lines pointing at the middle, the whole disc, one arm and a blue patch in an arm.

items.p: Match each person to what they found.
pairs: how a blinking star's rhythm tells you how far away it is
that Andromeda is a galaxy far outside the Milky Way
that the universe is growing and was once tiny and hot
the faint leftover glow from the hot early universe
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each step needed the one before. Hubble could only measure Andromeda's distance because of Leavitt's rule.

items.p: Andromeda is moving towards us, but almost every far galaxy is moving away. How can both be true?
items.a: Andromeda is close, so gravity between it and the Milky Way is strong enough to pull them together. Far galaxies are carried apart because the space between them stretches, and over such big distances gravity is too weak to stop it.
items.why: A strong answer names both things at work: gravity close by, and stretching space far away.

items.p: Which of these is a clue that the universe was once very hot?
opts: A faint glow of microwaves comes from every direction in the sky
The Sun is hot
Some stars are red
The Moon has craters
items.why: The faint glow is light left over from when the whole universe was hot. It has been stretched by the expanding universe into microwaves. The Sun is hot for its own reason: it joins hydrogen into helium deep inside.

items.p: In 1920, two astronomers held a famous debate. Nobody could yet measure how far away the spiral smudges in telescopes were.

views.says: The Milky Way is huge, and it is the whole universe. The spiral smudges are small clouds inside it.
The spiral smudges are other galaxies like ours, very far away.

items.ask: Who would you have agreed with in 1920, before anyone could measure the distance? Give a reason. Then say what Hubble found in 1923, and who it showed was right.
items.a: Either side can be argued in 1920. Shapley had measured that the Milky Way is very big, and a colleague claimed to have seen the smudges spin. Curtis noticed that exploding stars in the smudges looked very faint, as if far away. In 1923 Hubble found a Cepheid in Andromeda and showed it is far outside the Milky Way, so Curtis was right about this.
items.why: This was a real debate between careful scientists. It was settled by a new measurement, made possible by Henrietta Leavitt's work.

items.p: The Webb telescope has seen galaxies whose light set off more than 13 billion years ago. Why do these galaxies help us learn about the early universe?
items.a: We see them as they were more than 13 billion years ago, when the universe was young. So they show us what galaxies were like near the beginning.
items.why: A strong answer says that far light is old light, so far galaxies are pictures of the past.

items.p: On the balloon, only the rubber skin stood for space. The air inside and the room outside were not part of the model. Why does this matter when you use the balloon to think about the universe?
items.context: In the Bindi Balloon experiment, you stick bindis on a small balloon, measure the gaps between them with a thread, blow the balloon bigger, and measure again.
items.a: If you count the inside, the middle of the air looks like a centre. But the bindis live only on the skin, and on the skin there is no centre. The real universe has no inside or outside like the balloon. Every model gets some things wrong, so you have to know which parts count.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a model is useful only if we know which of its parts stand for real things.

items.p: On a bigger balloon, Meenakshi's bindi D started 4 times as far from home as bindi A. When the balloon grew, A moved 2 cm further away. About how far did D move?
opts: 2 cm
4 cm
8 cm
16 cm
items.why: D was 4 times as far, so it moves about 4 times as much: 4 times 2 is 8 cm. Hubble found the same rule for galaxies: four times as far away means moving away about four times as fast.
items.context: In the Bindi Balloon experiment, you stick bindis on a small balloon, measure the gaps between them with a thread, blow the balloon bigger, and measure again.

items.p: Imagine the stretching of the universe played backwards, like a film in reverse. What would happen to the galaxies? What would the universe be like at the start?
items.a: The galaxies would come closer and closer together. Everything would get packed tighter, and packed things get hotter. At the start, everything would be squeezed together and extremely hot. That is the Big Bang.
items.why: A strong answer goes step by step: closer, packed, hotter.

items.p: Nobody knows what came before the Big Bang. Here are three real answers people have given.

views.says: Time itself may have begun with the Big Bang. Asking what came before may be like asking what is north of the North Pole.
Our universe may have come after an earlier one, in a long chain of universes.

views.who: The Nasadiya Sukta, a hymn in the Rig Veda
views.says: Who really knows how this world came to be? Perhaps even the one who watches over it does not know.

items.ask: Which answer makes most sense to you? Give a reason. Then say one good thing about another answer.
items.a: Any choice can be strong if it gives a reason. For example, Hawking's answer explains why we can't look further back. Penrose's answer can perhaps be tested by looking for patterns in the leftover glow. The hymn is honest that the question may have no answer we can reach.
items.why: This is a real open question. Scientists do not agree, and none of the ideas has been tested yet.

items.p: The Big Bang happened at one spot in space, and the galaxies flew out from that spot.
items.why: False. The Big Bang happened everywhere at once. Every part of space, including the space where you are now, was part of the hot, packed early universe.

items.p: Sushila looks at a galaxy so far away that its light set off 1 billion years ago. What does she see?
opts: The galaxy as it is today
The galaxy as it was 1 billion years ago
Nothing, because the light is too old
items.why: Old light still shows a clear picture. It is a picture of how the galaxy was when the light set off. The galaxy may have changed a lot since then.

items.p: Most elliptical galaxies have very few young blue stars. Spiral galaxies have many, in their arms. What might this tell you about how much gas each kind has left for making new stars?
items.a: New stars are made from gas. Spirals still have plenty of gas, so they keep making new stars. Ellipticals have used up or lost most of their gas, so they make very few.
items.why: A strong answer links young stars to gas, and uses that to compare the two kinds.

items.p: Draw the Bindi Balloon twice, small and big. On the big one, draw arrows from one bindi to the others. Make the arrows longer where the bindis moved further.
items.a: Short arrows to near bindis and long arrows to far bindis, from any bindi chosen.
items.why: The arrows show the pattern Hubble found: the further away, the faster it moves away.
items.art: Two empty circles, one small and one big, side by side.

items.p: Sort these. Is each pair getting further apart as the universe expands, or held together by gravity?
items: two groups of galaxies very far apart
the stars inside the Milky Way
the furthest galaxy the Webb telescope has seen, and us
items.a: see items
items.why: The stretching wins only across the huge gaps between groups of galaxies. Close by, gravity and the forces that hold atoms together are much stronger.

items.p: The faint glow of microwaves that comes from every direction in the sky is called the cosmic microwave ____.
items.why: It is called the background because it lies behind everything else we see. It is the oldest light there is.

items.p: Dev, a boy in Class 3, says: 'Space is stretching, so my house must be stretching too.' What would you tell him?
items.a: Your house does not stretch. The stretching only shows across the huge gaps between groups of galaxies. Close by, the forces holding things together are far stronger. Even on the balloon, the bindis did not get bigger.
items.why: A strong answer uses the bindis as evidence and names what holds things together.

items.p: In 1929, Edwin Hubble compared how far away galaxies are with how fast they move away. What pattern did he find?
opts: The further away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away
The nearer a galaxy is, the faster it moves away
All galaxies move away at the same speed
Galaxies are not moving at all
items.why: Further away means faster. This is just what the bindis did. Today it is called the Hubble-Lemaître law, because Georges Lemaître had worked it out first, in 1927.

items.p: Put these in the order they happened, starting with the earliest.
items: The universe is extremely hot and packed together
The first stars and galaxies form
The Sun and the Earth form
The first living things appear on Earth
items.a: order shown
items.context: In the Universe in One Year activity, the whole 13.8 billion years of the universe is squeezed into one calendar year, so that each day stands for about 38 million years.
items.why: On the one-year calendar: 1 January, early January, about 1 September, late September, 30 December, and 31 December just before midnight.

items.p: Which one is not a clue that the universe had a hot beginning?
opts: Far galaxies are moving away from us
A faint microwave glow comes from every direction
The universe is mostly hydrogen and helium, in the amounts a hot beginning would make
Some galaxies are spirals and some are ellipticals
items.why: Galaxy shapes tell us how each galaxy grew, but not about the beginning. The other three are the main clues for the Big Bang.

items.p: Andromeda's light set off 2.5 million years ago. Someone in Andromeda, looking at the Earth today with a giant telescope, would see the Earth as it was then. What would they see?
items.a: They would see the Earth 2.5 million years ago. There would be no people like us, no cities and no lights. There were early relatives of humans in Africa, some making simple stone tools.
items.why: A strong answer uses the same idea both ways: light from us to them takes as long as light from them to us.

applications: Astronomers use Henrietta Leavitt's blinking stars as measuring sticks, to find how far away galaxies are.
India's AstroSat space telescope and the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune study far galaxies and the early universe.
The Planck spacecraft mapped the faint leftover glow, and from it scientists worked out that the universe is 13.8 billion years old.
Computer programs that sort galaxies by shape were trained using the sorting done by Galaxy Zoo volunteers.
Because far light is old light, astronomers can study how galaxies grew, by looking at galaxies at different distances.
In 2017, a team from Pune found a huge group of galaxies about 4 billion light-years away and named it the Saraswati supercluster.

open_questions.q: What came before the Big Bang, if anything?
open_questions.why_open: Our best theories stop working at the very start. Some scientists think time began then, and others think an earlier universe came first. None of the ideas has been tested.

open_questions.q: Why is the stretching of the universe speeding up?
open_questions.why_open: In 1998, astronomers found that the expansion is getting faster. They call the unknown cause 'dark energy', but nobody knows what it is.

open_questions.q: How did the first galaxies grow so big so quickly?
open_questions.why_open: The Webb telescope has found more bright galaxies in the young universe than many astronomers expected. They are working out whether their ideas about how galaxies grow need to change.

open_questions.q: Does the universe go on for ever, or does it have an edge?
open_questions.why_open: We can only see as far as light has had time to travel. Beyond that, nobody can look, so nobody knows how big the whole universe is.

open_questions.q: Will Andromeda and the Milky Way crash together?
open_questions.why_open: Andromeda is coming towards us. A study in 2025 found it is uncertain whether the two will merge in the next 10 billion years, because the pulls of other nearby galaxies are hard to measure.

maths.problem: In her Bindi Balloon test, Priya measured these gaps from home. Small balloon: A 3 cm, B 6 cm, C 9 cm. Big balloon: A 6 cm, B 12 cm, C 18 cm. How much further away did each bindi go? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: A went 3 cm further, B 6 cm and C 9 cm. Each bindi moved as far again as it started, so each gap doubled.
maths.explain: 6 take away 3 is 3. 12 take away 6 is 6. 18 take away 9 is 9. The bindi that started 3 times as far away moved 3 times as much.
maths.context: In the Bindi Balloon experiment, you stick bindis on a small balloon, measure the gaps between them with a thread, blow the balloon bigger, and measure again.

chart.title: How much further from home each bindi went

maths.why_maths: Taking away the before from the after shows how far each bindi moved, and comparing the answers shows the rule Hubble found.

maths.problem: On a piece of elastic, dots are at 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 cm from home. The elastic is stretched until it is 3 times as long. Where will each dot be? How far will the 10 cm dot have moved?
maths.answer: At 6, 12, 18, 24 and 30 cm. The 10 cm dot moves 20 cm.
maths.explain: Each distance is multiplied by 3: 2 times 3 is 6, and so on up to 10 times 3, which is 30. The 10 cm dot goes from 10 to 30, which is 20 cm.
maths.context: In the Stretch the Elastic activity, you mark dots 2 centimetres apart on a piece of elastic, tape one end down, and stretch it to twice its length.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying lets you predict where every dot goes without measuring, and then you can check the prediction with the ruler.

maths.problem: On the Universe in One Year calendar, the universe's 13,800 million years are squeezed into 12 months. About how many million years does each month stand for?
maths.answer: About 1,150 million years, a little more than a billion years.
maths.explain: 13,800 divided by 12 is 1,150. Check: 1,150 times 12 is 13,800.
maths.context: In the Universe in One Year activity, the whole 13.8 billion years of the universe is squeezed into one calendar year, so that each day stands for about 38 million years.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the huge age into equal parts turns it into months we can picture.

maths.problem: Light from Andromeda set off about 2,500,000 years ago. The first modern humans lived about 300,000 years ago. About how many times older is Andromeda's light than the oldest modern humans?
maths.explain: 300,000 times 8 is 2,400,000, which is close to 2,500,000. So the light is a little more than 8 times as old.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two big numbers shows how long the light was travelling before there were any people like us to see it.

maths.problem: Asha sorted 20 galaxy photos on Galaxy Zoo. She found 11 spirals, 6 smooth ovals and 3 that were something else. Draw a bar chart. Then say why some of her smooth ovals might really be spirals.
maths.answer: Bars of 11, 6 and 3. Some 'smooth ovals' might be spirals seen from a slant or far away, so their arms don't show.
maths.explain: 11 and 6 and 3 make 20. In the Tilt the Spiral test, the plate looked like an oval when tilted, and the arms were harder to see.
maths.context: In the Galaxy Zoo activity, you sort real galaxy photos on a website and keep a tally of their shapes.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which shape is most common, and then we can ask whether the count could be fooled.

roots.context: We have stretched a balloon, met the shapes of galaxies and learned that far light is old light. Now we ask what this says about where we are, and where everything came from.

deep_truth.truth: On your balloon, every bindi moved away from every other, and far ones moved furthest. No bindi was the centre. Galaxies move apart the same way, because the space between them stretches. So the Big Bang happened everywhere at once, including right where you sit.
deep_truth.habit: We picture the Big Bang as a bomb going off at one spot, with galaxies flying out like sparks. That picture puts a centre somewhere, and puts us off to one side. But the stretching happens everywhere at once, so there is no centre, and our place was part of the beginning like every other.
deep_truth.evidence: On the balloon, the bindi three times as far from home moved about three times as much, and the same was true from a second bindi. Hubble and Lemaître found this pattern in real galaxies: twice as far away means moving away about twice as fast, in every direction.

three.who_am_i: From every galaxy, the others seem to move away, just as from every bindi. So no place is the centre of the universe, and your place is as central as any other.
three.what_is_life: Living things are made of carbon, oxygen and other atoms that only stars can make. The first stars had to shine and explode before there were any. So the universe was already hundreds of millions of years old before life could begin anywhere.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is not standing still. The space between the galaxies grows every moment, and the light reaching us carries pictures of the past. The sky you see tonight shows many different times at once.

roots.thread: On the balloon there was no special bindi. Every one saw the same thing: the others moving away. Science found that every place in the universe is like this. No galaxy is the middle and none is the edge, and every place was part of the same hot beginning. People are one kind of life on one planet, in one galaxy among hundreds of billions, and that galaxy is in the middle exactly as much as every other.

teachings.teaching: The world has its centre everywhere and its edge nowhere.
teachings.link: Nicholas of Cusa, a German thinker, wrote this nearly 500 years before Hubble. On the balloon, every bindi could be called the centre, because from each one the others moved away.

teachings.teaching: Then there was neither being nor non-being. Who really knows where this world came from? The one who watches over it from the highest heaven perhaps knows, or perhaps does not know.
teachings.link: Science has traced the universe back 13.8 billion years, to a hot, packed beginning. Before that, it does not know either. The hymn asks the same question, and is just as honest about not knowing.

science.text: The universe is expanding, and about 13.8 billion years ago it was extremely hot and packed together.
No place in the universe is the centre. Astronomers see the same pattern of galaxies moving apart in every direction.
What came before the Big Bang, or whether there was any 'before', nobody knows.
Some physicists think the total energy of the universe may be exactly zero (Edward Tryon, 1973).

other_view.view: The Big Bang theory describes how the universe changed from a hot, packed state. It does not explain why there is a universe at all, and many scientists think that question lies outside science. Some, like Roger Penrose, think our Big Bang was not the start, and an earlier universe came before it.

The Bindi Balloon was thought through with a standard round party balloon: about 12 cm across when half blown and about 24 cm when nearly full, so gaps of 3, 6 and 9 cm on the fat middle become roughly 6, 12 and 18 cm, a difference a child can measure with thread and a ruler. how_we_found_out.story: About a hundred years ago, most astronomers thought our Milky Way was the whole universe. The faint spiral smudges seen in telescopes, called spiral nebulae, were thought to be small clouds inside it. Nobody could tell, because nobody could measure how far away they were. Henrietta Swan Leavitt found the way. She worked at Harvard College Observatory in the United States, measuring stars on thousands of glass photographs. She studied Cepheids, stars that get brighter and dimmer in a steady rhythm. In 1912 she showed that the slower a Cepheid blinks, the brighter it really is. So timing its blinks tells you its real brightness, and how faint it looks tells you how far away it is. Leavitt died in 1921. Two years later, Edwin Hubble found a Cepheid in the Andromeda nebula with a big telescope at Mount Wilson in California. Leavitt's rule showed it was far outside the Milky Way. Andromeda was a whole galaxy of its own. In 1929, Hubble showed that far galaxies are moving away from us, the faster the further they are. Georges Lemaître had worked this out in 1927, and he said the universe must once have been tiny and hot.
how_we_found_out.who: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, an American astronomer, Edwin Hubble, an American astronomer, and Georges Lemaître, a Belgian physicist and priest
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe, and that the spiral smudges were clouds inside it. A Cepheid star in Andromeda, measured with Leavitt's rule, showed Andromeda was a separate galaxy far outside ours.
